# Template reference

This reference covers the two YAML files a rimsky author writes: the **template**, which declares a node graph, and the **compose manifest**, which declares which templates and instances a project keeps in a deployment. Every key of both files appears below, with its type, its accepted values, and its effect.

## How rimsky reads both files

Both files parse under the same rules.

- **Unknown keys are errors.** The parser rejects any key it does not recognize and names it. A misspelled key fails the whole file; it is never ignored.
- **`${VAR}` expands from the environment.** Any `${NAME}` in the file is replaced with that environment variable's value before parsing. An unset variable fails the load and the error names every missing variable.
- **A template may inline a file.** Where a template value is the single-key mapping `source_file: <relative-path>`, rimsky replaces the mapping with the named file's contents as a string. The path resolves relative to the template's own directory; an absolute path, or one that escapes the directory, is an error.

Register a template with `rimsky template register <file>`. Check one without registering it with `rimsky template lint <file>`.

**`rimsky template lint` is not an offline check.** The verb uploads the template to a deployment and the control API does the work; with no deployment reachable it fails with a connection error. This is structural rather than incidental: findings name the deployment's `executors:` and `claim_producers:` blocks, so the same file lints clean against one deployment and fails against another. Lint does catch everything registration rejects — the two report the same finding paths on the same files — but an author in CI with no deployment cannot lint at all.

---

# The template

A template declares a graph of nodes. Each node names an executor to run, the attributes it consumes and produces, the claims it acquires, and the sibling signals it reacts to. Registering a template stores it under a content hash; deploying it makes it instantiable; creating an instance from it gives it params and a live message queue.

## Top-level keys

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | The template's name. Required; a blank or whitespace-only value fails registration. |
| `version` | string | A free-form version string. Required; a blank or whitespace-only value fails registration. |
| `description` | string | Prose for a human reader. Rimsky stores it and never acts on it. |
| `nodes` | list | The node definitions of the single implied graph. Use this form or `graphs:`, never both — declaring both fails registration with `graphs_and_nodes_both_set`. A template must declare at least one node. |
| `graphs` | list | Named graphs, one of which must be `main`. See [Graphs and sub-graphs](#graphs-and-sub-graphs). |
| `params_schema` | JSON Schema object | The schema for the params an instance supplies at creation. Rimsky compiles it at registration; a schema that does not compile fails. Every `{{params.<key>}}` directive in the template must name a key declared under `params_schema.properties`. |
| `params_redact` | list of strings | Param paths to mask in the instance read. Each entry is a dotted path (`db.password` reaches a nested key); the single entry `*` masks every top-level param. A masked value reads back as `[REDACTED]`. |
| `late_bind_services` | list of strings | Service names a node may reference before the deployment declares them. A late-bound name skips the registration check that the deployment's `executors:` or `claim_producers:` block declares it; the binary is supplied at run time, by `rimsky run --service <name>=<path>`. |
| `message_queue_mode` | `backlog` \| `coalesce` | How an instance's pending message queue behaves. `backlog` (the default) keeps every pending message. `coalesce` cancels every pending message on the instance each time a new one arrives. |
| `messages` | list | The message types instances of this template accept. See [Messages](#messages). |
| `publishers` | list | The publisher bindings instances of this template open. See [Publishers](#publishers). |
| `defaults.attributes.by_executor.<executor>.<key>` | any JSON value | A default value for attribute `<key>` on every node whose executor is `<executor>`. The executor name must match some node's effective executor, or registration fails. |

**`params_redact` masks one surface, not all of them.** `GET /v1/instances/{id}` returns the masked value, and so the instance listing, the frame reads, the node reads, the instance-filtered event query, and the process logs stay clean. Five reads return the param in full: `GET /v1/events`, `GET /v1/audit`, `GET /v1/observability/events`, `GET /v1/observability/instances/{id}`, and `GET /v1/observability/instances`. In the first three the carrier is an `auth.access_attempted` event whose payload holds the verbatim create request. In the two observability instance views it is the instance's raw params, sitting beside the masked copy the ordinary instance read returns to the same key. Any reader holding `event:read`, `audit:read`, or `observability:read` sees the value. Treat `params_redact` as suppression in the instance read, not as a secrets mechanism.

**`defaults.attributes` takes one selector, the instance takes three.** At template level only `by_executor` exists; writing `by_node` or `by_match` fails at YAML parse with an unknown-field error rather than a validation finding. Instance-level `attribute_overrides` accepts all three. An author factoring out per-node defaults must repeat them at every instance creation.

## Node keys

Each entry of `nodes:` (or of a graph's `nodes:`) is a node definition.

### Identity

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | The node's name, and how every other key addresses it. Required, and unique across the whole template — a duplicate across two graphs fails registration. |
| `description` | string | Prose for a human reader. |
| `tags` | list of strings | Labels attached to the node. Each entry may carry `{{params.<key>}}` directives, which resolve at instance creation; a tag directive of any other kind fails registration. |

**Node tags select over HTTP only.** `GET /v1/instances/{id}/nodes?tag=<value>` returns the matching nodes with their tags. No CLI verb that lists nodes accepts `--tag` or `--tag-prefix`, and `rimsky instance nodes -o json` does not print the tags at all. Where those flags do exist they select a different noun: `--tag` on `template register` attaches a template tag, and `--tag-prefix` on `template list` filters templates. An operator who tags nodes and then reaches for `--tag-prefix` filters templates and gets a plausible empty answer.

### Dispatch mode

A node picks exactly one dispatch mode. `executor`, `delegate`, and `sends_message` are mutually exclusive, and `kind` is incompatible with all three.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `executor` | string | The executor that runs this node, by the name the deployment's `executors:` block declares. An undeclared name fails registration unless it is listed in `late_bind_services`. |
| `kind` | string | Sugar for a bundled executor. Registration rewrites `kind` into the matching `executor`. The registered kinds at this release are `loop_counter`, `attribute_passthrough`, and `send_message`. An unregistered kind fails registration. |
| `delegate` | string | The name of a sub-graph in this template to dispatch as one child execution. The named graph must declare both `entry:` and `exit:`. A `delegate:` cycle across graphs fails with `subgraph_recursion_unsupported`. |
| `sends_message` | string | A message type from this template's `messages:` registry. The node builds one message envelope from its own attributes and inserts it into the instance's message ledger. The node's `attributes.schema` properties and its `required:` set must match the message type's `body_schema` exactly — same field names, same declared types, same required set. |

A node that declares none of the four is a pure cascade node. It acquires whatever claims and locks it declares, then settles with a success terminal without dispatching anything, so it exists to gate and fan a signal onward. Declaring attributes on such a node registers with a warning, because only an executor consumes attribute values.

### Subscriptions

`subscribes:` is a list. Each entry declares one signal the node reacts to.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `node` | string | The sender. Either a node `type` declared in this template, or a message type declared in `messages:`. Required. |
| `type` | string | The signal type-path to match. Required. See [Subscription signal types](#subscription-signal-types). |
| `when` | CEL expression | A predicate over the signal's payload. The subscription fires only when the predicate is true. |
| `force_upstream_refresh` | boolean | **Required — write `true` or `false` explicitly.** There is no default, and omitting it fails registration. `true` invalidates the sender so it re-runs in the same frame before this node dispatches. `false` leaves the sender where it is. |
| `resolves_via_calling_node` | boolean | Set by sub-graph canonicalization. An author who writes it fails registration. |

Two entries that share the same `(node, type, when)` triple must agree on `force_upstream_refresh`; conflicting values fail registration.

Subscribing is also waking. A matching emission from the sender always marks this node stale and gates its dispatch on the sender. There is no declaration that reads a sender's data without also waking on it.

A subscription whose `node` is a message type may only use `terminal/success` or `terminal/*`. Message delivery only ever manifests as `terminal/success`, so any other type can never fire, and registration rejects it.

**The `when:` predicate.** It compiles at registration and evaluates at cascade-walk time. Two variables bind: `type` (string) and `payload` (map). When `type:` is an exact path, field references parse-check against that signal's payload shape and an unknown field fails registration. When `type:` ends in `*`, `payload` binds dynamically and no field check runs. The CEL standard library is available; rimsky adds no helper functions. A predicate that errors at evaluation is treated as no-match.

The payload fields available per signal:

| Signal | Payload fields |
|---|---|
| `terminal/success` | `changed`, `attributes_delta`, `change_summary`, `tags` |
| `terminal/error/<class>` | `error_class`, `error_payload`, `attempt`, `retries_so_far`, `attributes_delta`, `tags` |
| `attribute/<key>/changed` | `key`, `value`, `old_value` |

Filter on a terminal tag by pairing a wildcard type with a predicate — `type: terminal/*` plus `when: '"needs-review" in payload.tags'`. Filter on an attribute the sender wrote with `payload.attributes_delta.<field>`.

### Attributes

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `attributes.schema` | JSON Schema object | The node's typed input and output bag. Rimsky compiles it at registration. |

The schema is ordinary JSON Schema with two rimsky-specific property keywords.

- **`source:`** — a string carrying one or more `{{...}}` directives. Rimsky resolves them at dispatch and populates the property with the result. See [The substitution grammar](#the-substitution-grammar).
- **`default:`** — a literal value used when nothing else populates the property.

A property may declare `source:` or `default:`, never both. Where the node's executor publishes an expected-attributes schema, every property must carry `source:`, carry `default:`, or be marked `readOnly: true` in the executor's schema — otherwise it is unpopulated at dispatch and registration says so. A property the template marks `readOnly: true` that the executor does not is an error; the executor is authoritative on which properties it produces.

Rimsky composes the effective schema from three layers, in order: the executor's expected-attributes schema, `defaults.attributes.by_executor`, then the node's own `attributes.schema`. A property type the node declares must equal the executor's declared type. Where the executor's schema is closed (`additionalProperties: false`), a property neither the executor nor the node declares is an error. The composed default values are validated against the executor's schema.

**Every substitution ref must be covered by a subscription.** A `{{nodes.<sender>.attribute.<key>}}` ref requires a `subscribes:` entry on this node for that sender with type `attribute/<key>/changed` or `attribute/*`. A `{{messages.<type>...}}` ref requires an entry for that message type with `terminal/success` or `terminal/*`. An uncovered ref fails registration, and the finding carries the exact `subscribes:` entry to add.

### Claims and locks

`claim_producers:` is a list. Each entry acquires one claim for the duration of the node's run.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | The claim producer, by the name the deployment's `claim_producers:` block declares. Required. An undeclared name fails registration unless it is listed in `late_bind_services`. |
| `selector` | string | What to acquire, in the producer's own vocabulary. Required. May carry `{{...}}` directives, resolved at acquisition. |
| `intent` | `r` \| `rw` | Read or read-write. Required; any other value fails registration. |
| `alias` | string | The local name this claim answers to in `{{claim.<alias>...}}` directives, in `holds:` on other nodes, and in `fan_out.claim`. Defaults to `name`. Two claims on one node may not resolve to the same alias. |
| `lifetime` | `subgraph` \| `durable` | `subgraph` (the default) commits or abandons the claim when the holding sub-graph completes, and the retention sweep later reaps the row. `durable` commits the same way but exempts the row from the sweep, so it survives for later runs to co-hold and for asset queries; releasing it takes an explicit operator action. |
| `data` | JSON | An opaque blob passed through to the producer's open verb. Rimsky never inspects it. |

`locks:` is a list of named-lock references.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | A named lock, by the name the deployment's `named_locks:` block declares. Required and unique within the node; an undeclared name fails registration. It may carry `{{...}}` directives, resolved at acquisition — a name that carries one skips the declared-name check, because the final name is known only at dispatch. |

`holds:` is a mapping. Each key is a claim alias belonging to another node; the node co-holds that node's claim rather than acquiring its own.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `<alias>.from` | string | The node that acquired the claim. Required. The named node must declare `<alias>` in its own `claim_producers:` block. A node may not hold from itself, and the holds graph must be acyclic. |
| `<alias>.as` | string | A local rename for the held claim. Defaults to `<alias>`. Two entries may not resolve to the same local name. |

### Error handling

`error_types:` is a mapping from an error class to a policy. Rimsky looks the class up when a dispatch ends in an error.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `<class>.action` | `pass` \| `give_up` \| `retry` \| `release_and_requeue` | Required. `pass` settles the run fresh, treating the error as benign downstream. `give_up` settles the run failed. `retry` re-invokes the executor in place, keeping the claims, the attribute bag, and the dispatch id. `release_and_requeue` releases the run's claims and re-enqueues it for a fresh acquire. |
| `<class>.reason` | string | The label recorded on a give-up. Rimsky reads it only under `action: give_up`; elsewhere it has no effect. |

**Lookup is an exact match on the class name, so there is no catch-all.** A bare `*` entry, or `http/*`, registers with a warning that the class is not in any declared vocabulary — and then routes nothing. A node whose only entry is a wildcard behaves exactly like a node with no `error_types:` at all: default handling for every class, which is give-up. Enumerate the classes you mean to route.

Without a matching entry, rimsky gives up. Fail-fast is the default and retry is opt-in. A node that declares `claim_producers:` but no `acquire/unavailable` entry registers with a warning saying exactly that.

Rimsky range-checks each class against the union of the vocabularies it can see — the node's executor's declared classes, the declared classes of every producer in the node's `claim_producers:` block, and the runtime-synthesized classes (`template_resolution_failed`, `template_validation_failed`, `executor_schema_unavailable`, `attributes_schema_failed`, `unresolved_executor`, `executor_sync_timeout`, `executor_protocol_violation`, `abandoned`, and any class under `acquire/`). A class no vocabulary declares is a warning, never a rejection.

### Retries and backoff

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `max_retries` | integer | The retry budget for one dispatch, counted across every error class in that dispatch. Unset means unbounded. Exhausting the budget synthesizes a give-up with reason `max_retries_exhausted`. |
| `retry_backoff.kind` | `linear` \| `exponential` | `linear` waits `base_delay_ms × attempt`. `exponential` waits `base_delay_ms × 2^(attempt-1)`. Any other value fails registration. |
| `retry_backoff.jitter` | `none` \| `plus_minus` | `plus_minus` scales the computed delay by a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5. Any other value fails registration. |
| `retry_backoff.base_delay_ms` | integer | The base delay. Must be positive whenever any other `retry_backoff` key is set — a zero base makes every computed delay zero — and may never be negative. |
| `retry_backoff.max_delay_ms` | integer | A ceiling on the computed delay. Unset or `0` means no ceiling. It may not be negative, and it may not sit below `base_delay_ms`. |

**Retry policy is per-node only.** `max_retries` and the four `retry_backoff` keys have no deployment-wide form. Writing either under `dispatch_defaults` in deployment configuration stops the deployment before it starts: migrate exits with an unknown-field error and the entrypoint reports `migrate failed`. Only `sync_rpc_deadline`, `max_quiet_period`, and `max_runtime` have a `dispatch_defaults` counterpart.

### Deadlines

Three independent deadlines bound a dispatch. Each takes a duration string (`30s`, `5m`, `1h30m`). `0` disables the deadline. Any non-zero value below one second fails registration, as does a negative one.

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sync_rpc_deadline` | Bounds a synchronous dispatch's outbound call. It is the only bound on that call; no executor-internal timeout sits beneath it. |
| `max_quiet_period` | The maximum time between liveness signals during an asynchronous dispatch. |
| `max_runtime` | An absolute wall-clock bound on the dispatch. |

### Fan-out

`fan_out:` partitions a held claim and dispatches one child execution per partition.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `claim` | string | The claim alias to partition, from this node's `claim_producers:` or `holds:`. Required. Its producer must advertise `supports_split_scope`, or registration fails. |
| `partition_request` | string | An opaque request handed to the producer's split verb, after `{{...}}` substitution. Required. |
| `parallelism` | integer | How many children run at once. `0` means unlimited. A negative value fails registration. |
| `error_policy.kind` | `strict` \| `threshold` \| `best_effort` \| `first` | How child outcomes aggregate into the parent's. Defaults to `strict`. Under `strict`, one child's abandon force-abandons its in-flight siblings. |
| `error_policy.max_failures` | integer | The failure tolerance under `kind: threshold`. Must be greater than zero when that kind is set. |

### Cascade mode

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `cascade_mode` | `most-recent` \| `sequenced` \| `idempotent-queue` \| `idempotent-settled` | How re-cascades onto this node behave within one frame. Defaults to `most-recent`. Any other value fails registration. |

- `most-recent` — an unclaimed earlier round is deleted, and the newest round survives.
- `sequenced` — no round is ever dropped; queued rounds dispatch one at a time, in order.
- `idempotent-queue` — a round whose resolved inputs are byte-identical to the most recent prior round is dropped.
- `idempotent-settled` — the same comparison, extended to the most-recently-settled successful run when no prior round exists.

Every mode compares only within the current frame. No mode reads a prior frame's run.

### Keys rimsky sets for itself

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
| `is_subgraph_entry_absorbed` | Set when a delegating node absorbs its sub-graph's entry. An author who writes it fails registration. |
| `is_subgraph_exit` | Set on the node a sub-graph names as its `exit:`. An author who writes it fails registration. |

## Graphs and sub-graphs

Use `graphs:` instead of top-level `nodes:` when a template has more than one graph.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | The graph's name. Required and unique. Exactly one graph must be named `main`. |
| `entry` | string | The node a delegating caller absorbs. Required on every graph except `main`, forbidden on `main`, and must name a node this graph declares. |
| `exit` | string | The node whose settlement settles the delegation. Required on every graph except `main`, forbidden on `main`, must name a node this graph declares, and must differ from `entry`. |
| `nodes` | list | The graph's node definitions, in the shape described above. |

Sub-graphs are closed. A node inside a sub-graph may only `subscribes:` or `holds:` from nodes in the same sub-graph, and a `main`-graph node may not reach a sub-graph's internals at all — `delegate:` plus the entry/exit rule is the only way in and out. Every node of a sub-graph other than `entry` and `exit` must be reachable from `entry` and able to reach `exit` along subscription edges.

Delegation absorbs the entry node into the caller. The caller inherits the entry's executor, and the entry's claims, holds, and attribute schema merge into the caller's. A claim alias or holds alias declared on both sides with different bindings fails with `subgraph_absorption_alias_conflict`; rename one side.

## Messages

`messages:` declares the message types instances of this template accept.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | The message type-path. Required. It must contain at least one `/` so it cannot collide with a node type, must not start or end with `/`, must have no empty segment, must contain no whitespace, and no segment may contain `.` — the directive parser splits on `.`. It must not duplicate another message type or match a node type. The empty type is reserved for the implicit wake trigger rimsky seeds at registration. |
| `body_schema` | JSON Schema object | The message body's shape. Rimsky compiles it at registration; a schema that is not a JSON object, or does not compile, fails. Omit it for an empty body. |

A node subscribes to a message type by naming it in `subscribes[].node`, and reads its fields with `{{messages.<type>.<field>}}`. A `when:` predicate on a message subscription checks `payload.attributes_delta.<field>` references against the declared `body_schema`.

## Publishers

`publishers:` declares the publisher bindings an instance opens. A publisher is a peer service that pushes messages into the instance.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | The publisher peer, by the name the deployment declares. Required and unique within the template. |
| `kind` | string | Which of that peer's advertised kinds to use. Required. A kind the peer does not advertise in its capabilities handshake fails registration and the finding lists what it does advertise. The bundled sensors advertise `cron`, `http`, `object-store`, and `webhook`. |
| `config` | JSON | The binding's configuration, in the shape that kind defines. Rimsky passes it through. |
| `message_type` | string | The message type the publisher's emissions arrive as. Required and non-empty, and it must be declared in this template's `messages:` registry. |

## The substitution grammar

Rimsky substitutes `{{...}}` directives in five places: `attributes.schema` property `source:` values, `claim_producers[].selector`, `locks[].name`, `fan_out.partition_request`, and `tags`. The first four resolve at dispatch; `tags` resolve once, at instance creation, and accept only `params.` directives. Only the double-brace form is substituted; a bare `{params.<key>}` passes through unchanged.

Six directive kinds exist.

| Directive | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `{{params.<key>}}` | An instance param. `<key>`'s top segment must be declared under `params_schema.properties`. |
| `{{nodes.<node>.attribute.<key>}}` | An upstream node's attribute. `<node>` must be a declared node and `<key>` must be declared in that node's `attributes.schema` properties. |
| `{{messages.<type>.<field>}}` | A field of a message of that type delivered to this frame. `<type>` must be declared in `messages:` and `<field>` in its `body_schema`. With no such message bound to the frame, the dispatch fails. |
| `{{claim.<alias>.address}}`, `{{claim.<alias>.claim_scope}}`, `{{claim.<alias>.payload[.<field>]}}` | Part of an acquired claim. `<alias>` must come from this node's `claim_producers:` or `holds:`. `address` and `claim_scope` take no further path. |
| `{{child.partition_key}}` | The partition key of the current fan-out child. Takes no further path. |
| `{{env.<VAR_NAME>}}` | A process environment variable of the supervisor, read at dispatch. The name must match `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`. An unset variable fails the dispatch. |

Two modifiers handle a missing value, and a directive uses at most one of them.

- **`{{<directive> | <literal>}}`** substitutes the literal when the directive resolves to nothing. The literal is `null`, `true`, `false`, a JSON number, or a double-quoted string. One pipe only; a chain of fallbacks fails registration.
- **`{{<directive>?}}`** substitutes null when the directive resolves to nothing.

Writing both — `{{params.x? | "d"}}` — fails registration, because `?` says null and `|` says the literal.

A `source:` value must contain at least one directive; a literal string is an error. It may contain more than one, and it may mix directives with surrounding text, in which case the result is the interpolated string.

## Subscription signal types

A `subscribes[].type` names a signal type-path, either exactly or with a single trailing `*`. A positional wildcard such as `terminal/*/x` fails registration.

Three families exist, and only two of them are subscribable.

| Type | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `terminal/success` | The sender's run ends successfully. |
| `terminal/error/<class>` | The sender's run ends in an error of that class. `<class>` may itself contain `/`. `terminal/error/abandoned` is the class the runtime emits when a held claim resolves to abandon. |
| `attribute/<key>/changed` | The sender wrote a value for `<key>` that differs from the same node's prior run in the same run-scope. A key present before and absent now emits with `value: null`. |

The useful wildcards are `terminal/*` (any settlement), `terminal/error/*` (any error), `terminal/error/<prefix>*` (a family of classes), and `attribute/*` (any attribute write).

**`transient/*` signals are audit-only and cannot be subscribed to.** They record moments when one dispatch concluded but the run continues — a retry, an infra fault, a release-and-requeue, an async-callback deferral, a park. They write to the audit ledger and fire no cascade. Registration rejects a subscription against any of them, and rejects `transient/park` with an explicit message: subscribe to the eventual `terminal/success` or `terminal/error/<class>` instead.

A node with no upstream of any kind — no `subscribes:` entry to another node, no upstream attribute substitution, no message-body consumption — is a structural root. Rimsky injects a wake edge for it at registration, so an empty message starts it.

# The compose manifest

A compose manifest declares a project's templates and instances. `rimsky compose plan` prints what would change, `rimsky compose up` applies it, `rimsky compose down` removes it, `rimsky compose status` reports what is in the manifest, and `rimsky compose run` brings up a self-hosted one-shot stack and drives the manifest to terminal.

Compose namespaces everything it owns under the reserved tag prefix `compose:<project>:`, so its resources stay disjoint from anything you create by hand. A template tag you write in the manifest must not carry that prefix — compose adds it.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `project` | string | The project name, and the namespace for every tag and instance key compose creates. Required, and must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,62}$`. |
| `context` | string | A CLI context name to pin the manifest to a deployment. Must match `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._-]{0,62}$`. The pinned context wins over `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL` and over the CLI's configured default. Passing `--endpoint` alongside it is an error unless the two resolve to the same address. |
| `templates[].path` | string | The template file, relative to the manifest. Required and unique within the manifest. |
| `templates[].tag` | string | The tag compose attaches, before prefixing. Required and unique within the manifest. It must match `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9._:@/-]{0,254}$`, must not look like a `sha256-…` hash, and must not start with `compose:`. |
| `templates[].state` | `registered` \| `deployed` | How far to take the template. Defaults to `deployed`. |
| `instances[].name` | string | The instance's name within the project. Required, unique within the manifest, and must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,62}$`. |
| `instances[].template` | string | Which template to instantiate: a `tag` declared elsewhere in this manifest, or a literal `sha256-<64 hex>` template hash. Anything else fails validation. |
| `instances[].params` | mapping | The params passed at instance creation, checked against the template's `params_schema`. |
| `instances[].restart` | `never` \| `on_failure` \| `always` | What the next apply does with this instance once it has terminated. Defaults to `never`. |

**`templates[].state` only moves a template forward.** `state: registered` on a template that is already deployed parses and does nothing — the apply reports no changes and the template stays deployed. There is no manifest value that walks a template back; `undeployed` is not accepted and the file is refused outright with `must be one of registered|deployed`. Removing the template's entry, by contrast, does undeploy, untag, and delete it in one apply.

Removing an instance entry while that instance is still live refuses the whole run — `compose-owned non-terminal instances not in manifest` — and that refusal blocks every other change in the manifest, not only the instance's own. Wait for the instance to reach a terminal state, then apply.

**`restart` is not a supervision policy.** Nothing watches an instance between applies; `compose up` is a one-shot reconciler that exits, and no process re-creates an instance when it terminates. `compose status` reports an instance as in-manifest whether it is running or dead. The key is read only by the next hand-run `compose up`, which classifies an already-terminated instance: `always` deletes and re-creates it, `on_failure` re-creates it when its node runs aggregate to a failure and deletes it otherwise, and `never` does not re-create it.

An apply warns on params drift rather than acting on it. The control API has no in-flight instance update, so changing `instances[].params` under a running instance prints a warning and changes nothing.

## Peer blocks

`executors:` and `claim_producers:` are mappings keyed by service name. Each name must match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,62}$`.

`rimsky compose run` reads these blocks and writes them into the configuration of the stack it brings up. `compose plan`, `up`, `down`, and `status` validate them and otherwise ignore them, because those verbs reconcile against a deployment that already carries its own peer configuration.

| Key | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `executors.<name>.transport` | `grpc` \| `http` | How to reach the executor. Required. |
| `executors.<name>.endpoint` | string | The address. Required. |
| `executors.<name>.tls` | `off` \| `required` | The TLS posture. |
| `executors.<name>.protocols` | list of strings | Which protocols this peer serves. Each entry must be one of `claim_producer`, `executor`, `publisher`, `lifecycle_subscriber`, `validation`, `data_processing`. |
| `executors.<name>.observability_endpoint` | string | The address of the peer's observability sibling. |
| `claim_producers.<name>.endpoint` | string | The address. Required. |
| `claim_producers.<name>.write_semantics_allowed` | list | Which write semantics this producer permits. Required and non-empty. Each entry must be one of `sync`, `staged_async`, `blocking_async`, `read_only`. |
| `claim_producers.<name>.tls` | `off` \| `required` | The TLS posture. |
| `claim_producers.<name>.protocols` | list of strings | Which protocols this peer serves, from the same six names as above. |
| `claim_producers.<name>.observability_endpoint` | string | The address of the peer's observability sibling. |

`rimsky compose run` also reads a sibling `rimsky.yml` next to the manifest, if one exists, and carries its `publishers:` and `named_locks:` blocks into the stack it brings up.
